claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
subclaims: What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?
What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?
Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?
Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?
Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?
Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?
How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?

experiments: To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims about elimination vs bypass, run a mechanistic comparison on a public safety-aligned open-weight model such as Llama-2-Chat, Llama-3-Instruct, or Qwen2.5-Instruct using harmful/refusal benchmarks from HuggingFace or JailbreakBench plus benign controls from Anthropic HH-RLHF or WildChat. First, collect three prompt conditions for the same harmful intent: direct harmful request that is refused, jailbreak-wrapped harmful request that is complied with, and benign request. Record layerwise residual-stream activations and attention-head outputs for all conditions. Then train simple linear probes only on the refused-harmful vs benign contrast at each layer/head family, and test those probes zero-shot on jailbreak-successful harmful prompts. If probes trained to detect harmful intent in the refused condition still score jailbreaked harmful inputs as harmful at high AUROC, while the model behavior changes from refusal to compliance, that supports bypass rather than elimination. If probe scores collapse on jailbreaked harmful inputs toward benign levels, that supports elimination or severe corruption of safety-relevant representations. A useful extension is representational similarity analysis or CCA between refused-harmful and jailbreak-harmful internal states after controlling for lexical overlap; persistent similarity in harm-related directions despite different outputs would strengthen the bypass interpretation. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already public mechanistic traces showing layerwise harmful-intent probes remain active during successful jailbreaks across multiple models and attack families.

To address subclaim "What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?" identify whether successful jailbreaks consistently reduce activity in a small subset of attention heads. Using the same public models and prompt sets, compute per-head metrics under refused harmful prompts versus matched successful jailbreak prompts: attention output norm, direct logit attribution to refusal tokens, causal effect from head ablation, and activation patching score. Rank heads by the drop in these metrics during jailbreak success, and test whether the same small set recurs across prompts, attack templates, and models. To avoid confounding from token-position differences, compare within matched prompt pairs and use token-aligned windows near the model’s decision to refuse or comply. If a compact subset of heads shows large, reproducible suppression specifically when jailbreaks succeed, that supports the claim of selective suppression. If suppression is diffuse across many heads or concentrated in MLPs or residual-stream directions instead, the subclaim is weakened or revised. If no stable suppressed subset appears across attacks, then the mechanism may be attack-specific rather than general. This experiment would be partly unnecessary if prior evidence already provided robust, cross-model causal maps of refusal-related heads and showed jailbreaks consistently downregulate exactly those heads.

To address subclaim "Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?" perform direct causal interventions on the candidate suppressed heads found in the previous experiment. On harmful prompts that the aligned model normally refuses, ablate, zero, mean-replace, or scale down only the identified heads during generation, leaving the rest of the network unchanged. Measure the change in refusal rate, harmful compliance rate, and generation quality on benign prompts. Include controls that suppress an equal number of randomly selected heads, the next-best-ranked heads, and matched-norm heads. If suppressing just the candidate subset reliably converts refusals into harmful compliance far more often than control head sets, that strongly supports sufficiency. If many larger head sets or random sets cause similar compliance, then the claim that a small specific subset is sufficient is weakened. If suppression merely degrades coherence without increasing harmful compliance, then those heads may correlate with refusal rather than cause it. This experiment becomes less necessary if existing intervention studies already show that ablating a compact refusal-head circuit reproducibly flips outputs from refusal to compliance with minimal side effects.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?" test whether heads outside the suppressed subset still encode harmfulness during successful jailbreaks. Build head-level or layer-level readouts from the non-suppressed components only, again trained on refused-harmful vs benign prompts or using unsupervised directions such as mean-difference vectors between harmful and benign conditions. Evaluate these readouts on successful jailbreak prompts, and perform causal tracing or activation patching to confirm that information about harmful intent is localized in non-suppressed heads during those runs. One can also decode structured attributes of the harmful request, such as weapon/drug/self-harm category from public moderation datasets like OpenAI Moderation-style public replicas on HuggingFace, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, or WildGuardMix, using only activations from non-suppressed heads. If non-suppressed heads retain strong decodable harmfulness and category information during jailbreak success, this supports the persistence claim. If harmful information becomes largely undecodable outside the suppressed heads, then bypass is less plausible and stronger representational collapse is indicated. This experiment could be shortened if previous analyses already demonstrated that harm-relevant information remains linearly decodable from residual or head activations after the refusal circuit is disabled.

To address subclaim "Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?" and "Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?" evaluate training-free detectors built from internal representations on public harmfulness datasets such as BeaverTails, ToxicChat, WildGuardMix, JailbreakBench, and benign instruction datasets from Alpaca or UltraChat. Construct zero-training scores using methods like cosine similarity to a harm direction estimated from a small fixed public prompt set, nearest-neighbor scoring from a frozen bank of harmful vs benign exemplars, logit-lens scoring onto refusal-related vocabulary, or direct use of a previously identified residual direction without fitting new classifier weights on the evaluation data. Critically, separate any calibration prompts from test datasets and report AUROC, AUPRC, calibration, and robustness to paraphrase and jailbreak wrappers. If these no-additional-training detectors achieve strong discrimination on held-out harmful inputs, especially successful jailbreak prompts, the claim is supported. If acceptable detection requires fitting a learned probe or substantial labeled calibration, the no-additional-training subclaim is weakened. If performance is brittle across domains, the direct-readout idea may still hold only narrowly. This experiment would be less necessary if a public benchmark already showed frozen internal-direction scores transfer well across multiple harmfulness datasets without any fitted classifier.

To address subclaim "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?" benchmark the best training-free internal detector against public safety classifiers and moderation models on the same held-out datasets and jailbreak sets. Candidate baselines should include open models such as Llama Guard, WildGuard, Aegis, ShieldGemma, or other public moderation checkpoints available on HuggingFace, plus simple lexical baselines. Evaluate standard metrics overall and by slice: direct harmful prompts, successful jailbreak prompts, benign prompts containing harmful words in non-actionable contexts, multilingual subsets if available, and adversarial paraphrases. Also compare compute cost and latency, since an internal detector may be cheaper if it reuses the base model’s activations. If the internal detector matches or exceeds dedicated safety models on AUROC/AUPRC and maintains robustness on jailbreak-success cases, the competitiveness claim is supported. If it trails substantially except on narrow slices, then the claim should be narrowed. If it only works on the same model it is extracted from while safety models transfer better across models and domains, that is an important limitation. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already a public head-to-head benchmark showing frozen-representation detectors are competitive with current open moderation models across standard harmfulness and jailbreak evaluations.

To address subclaim 1/2/3 — what happens to safety-relevant internal representations during a successful jailbreak, and whether they are eliminated or bypassed — run a representational persistence study on a public safety-aligned open model such as Llama-2-7b-chat or Llama-3-Instruct using public harmful/benign prompt sets from AdvBench, HarmBench, and JailbreakBench. Construct matched prompt triplets: (a) harmful prompts that elicit refusal, (b) the same harmful prompts wrapped in successful jailbreak templates that elicit compliance, and (c) benign controls. For each model layer and attention head/residual stream position, extract activations under teacher forcing on the prompt and first generated token. Then quantify whether harmfulness information remains linearly decodable across conditions by training a simple decoder only on the refusal condition and testing zero-shot on the successful-jailbreak condition, and vice versa; also compare centered kernel alignment or representational similarity between harmful-refusal and harmful-jailbreak activations relative to benign prompts. If harmfulness remains decodable and harmful-refusal/harmful-jailbreak states are more similar to each other than either is to benign, that supports persistence/bypass rather than elimination. If decodability collapses specifically under successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination or severe transformation. If this experiment finds only partial persistence, later causal experiments should localize which components preserve it. This experiment could become partly unnecessary if there were already layer- and head-resolved public activation datasets for the same prompts showing cross-condition harmfulness decodability.

To address subclaim 4/5 — what the jailbreak attack selectively suppresses, and whether suppressing a small subset of attention heads is sufficient to turn refusal into compliance — perform a causal mediation and intervention analysis over attention heads. Using the same public models and datasets, first identify candidate safety-supporting heads by activation patching/path patching between refusal and jailbreak runs, prioritizing heads whose corrupted-to-clean patching most restores refusal logits or reduces attack success rate. Then intervene directly: on non-jailbroken harmful prompts that ordinarily trigger refusal, zero or down-scale only the top-k candidate heads during generation, varying k from 1 upward, and measure refusal rate, attack success rate, and helpfulness on benign tasks (e.g., AlpacaEval or MT-Bench subsets). The key test is whether a very small set of heads is sufficient to flip many refusals into compliance without broad model collapse. If suppressing a handful of heads sharply increases compliance on harmful requests while leaving benign capability mostly intact, that strongly supports the claim. If only large-scale ablation works, the claim that a small subset is sufficient is weakened. If no head subset reliably flips behavior, the selective-suppression account is undermined. This experiment could be made less necessary by stronger pre-existing evidence consisting of public causal head rankings replicated across multiple models and jailbreak families.

To address subclaim 6 — whether other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds — run a head-level residual representation audit after removing the causally implicated safety heads from analysis. For successful jailbreak prompts, estimate each head’s contribution to harmfulness information using logit lens projections, head-wise linear probes, or sparse readouts from each head output into a harmful-vs-benign label, but train the readout only on heads not implicated in refusal execution from Experiment 2. Then test whether these non-suppressed heads still encode harmfulness under successful jailbreaks. A stronger version is to ablate the identified safety heads during inference and then ask whether harmfulness remains decodable from the remaining heads/residual stream. If substantial harmfulness information remains in non-suppressed heads even after the safety heads are neutralized, that supports the idea that jailbreaks bypass refusal circuits while leaving content recognition elsewhere intact. If harmfulness decodability vanishes once those few heads are removed, that suggests the same small circuit both recognizes harmfulness and drives refusal, contrary to the claim. This experiment would be less necessary if published circuit analyses already separated harmfulness-recognition heads from refusal-execution heads with robust causal validation.

To address subclaim 7/8 — whether the persistent representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector and whether doing so requires no additional training — evaluate training-free or nearly training-free readouts from internal activations. Using public datasets such as HarmBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, and benign instruction sets, derive a harmfulness score from internal states without fitting a classifier on harmfulness labels: for example, use cosine similarity to a direction defined by the mean activation difference between clearly harmful and clearly benign exemplars from another dataset or use nearest-neighbor retrieval among stored harmful/benign activation centroids computed once from a disjoint source corpus; then freeze this rule and evaluate on unseen models/prompts/jailbreak templates. To respect the “no additional training” claim, avoid optimizing any parameters on the target dataset; calibration can be limited to an unsupervised threshold such as equal-error-rate estimated on benign-only data, or report threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC. If a simple frozen readout from persistent activations performs well on unseen jailbreaked harmful prompts, that supports direct readability without task-specific training. If good performance requires supervised probe fitting on the target data, then the “no additional training” portion is not supported. This experiment could be partly replaced by stronger evidence if prior work released fixed harmfulness directions or centroids that already generalize across datasets and jailbreak families.

To address subclaim 9 — how the quality of the internal-representation-based harmful-input detector compares with dedicated safety models — benchmark the best detector from Experiment 4 against public safety baselines such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, OpenAI moderation-style open surrogates if available, and standard fine-tuned classifiers on public datasets. Evaluate on mixed distributions containing direct harmful prompts, obfuscated/jailbroken harmful prompts, benign prompts with risky keywords, and benign adversarial confounders, using HarmBench, JailbreakBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, and WildGuard-style public sets if available. Report AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at matched false-positive rates, calibration, transfer across jailbreak families, and latency/compute cost. If the training-free internal detector is competitive with dedicated safety models across these metrics, especially on jailbreaked prompts, that supports the final claim. If it is substantially worse or only competitive after supervised tuning, the claim should be narrowed. This experiment becomes less necessary if a directly comparable public benchmark already includes both internal-state detectors and dedicated safety models evaluated under identical splits and attack families.

With respect to evidence piece “a small subset of attention heads located in the middle-to-late layers ... play a critical role” and the literature’s distinction between harmfulness recognition and refusal execution, run a cross-model, cross-attack replication study to test generality rather than existence in a single setup. Use several open aligned models (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2B-it/9B-it if accessible) and several jailbreak families from JailbreakBench or HarmBench (continuation-triggered, roleplay, translation/encoding, suffix, many-shot). Repeat Experiments 1–4 in a reduced form for each model/attack pair, then meta-analyze whether the same qualitative pattern recurs: persistent harmfulness representations, a small causally important head subset, and competitive readout quality. If the pattern is consistent across architectures and jailbreak styles, feasibility of the overall claim is much stronger. If it appears only for one model or one jailbreak family, the claim is likely overstated and should be scoped narrowly. This experiment could be deferred if earlier experiments already fail, or made less necessary by broad public replications from independent groups.

To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims about elimination vs bypass, run a representational comparison study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-Chat using harmful prompts from AdvBench and JailbreakBench under two conditions: (1) the harmful prompt alone, which usually yields refusal, and (2) the same harmful intent embedded in successful jailbreak prompts drawn from JailbreakBench or generated by GCG. Use deterministic decoding, validate attack success with a human-calibrated judge, and record layer/head activations during the prompt and first response tokens. First identify a "safety representation" using only the refusal condition, for example by finding directions, heads, or sparse feature groups that reliably separate harmful from harmless prompts while controlling for topic and length using harmless Alpaca prompts plus matched benign paraphrases. Then test whether those same representations remain linearly decodable in successful jailbreak runs, and whether their geometry is preserved via CKA / cosine similarity / probe transfer from refusal to jailbreak conditions. A key control is to compare against random subspaces and against non-adversarial harmful prompts that already fail or comply. If harmfulness remains decodable at similar levels during successful jailbreaks, that supports bypass rather than elimination; if decodability collapses specifically in successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination or severe rewriting of safety representations. If only some layers lose signal while others preserve it, the claim may need refinement toward partial bypass. This experiment becomes less necessary if strong prior evidence already shows stable cross-condition decoding of harmfulness at multiple layers and with multiple representational metrics.

To address subclaim "What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?" run a head-level causal attribution study comparing successful jailbreak prompts to matched non-jailbreak harmful prompts on the same model. Use activation/attribution patching and path patching across all attention heads to estimate each head’s contribution to refusal behavior, measuring effects on next-token refusal logits, KL divergence to the refusal run, and final ASR. Then compute differential activity and causal effect for each head between refusal and jailbreak conditions, ranking heads by both reduced activation and reduced causal contribution under jailbreak. Include controls demanded by the field: size-matched random head sets, layer-matched random head sets, and alternative circuit-discovery baselines such as simple activation magnitude ranking or sparse pruning. Also test whether the implicated heads are specific to harmfulness/refusal by evaluating the same interventions on harmless Alpaca prompts. If a small, reproducible subset of heads shows strongly reduced causal contribution specifically during successful jailbreaks, that supports selective suppression. If suppression is diffuse across many heads or equally observed for random sets, the claim of a small targeted subset is weakened. If the same heads matter broadly for helpfulness or coherence on harmless prompts, the effect may reflect generic capability disruption rather than safety-specific suppression. This experiment could be partly obviated by pre-existing robust circuit maps of refusal heads that have already been shown to drop out under jailbreak conditions across models.

To address subclaim "Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?" perform direct sufficiency and necessity interventions on the head subset identified in the previous experiment. On harmful prompts that normally produce refusals without jailbreaks, zero those heads or scale them down over a sweep w in {1, 0.5, 0, -0.5} during inference and measure changes in refusal logits, KL to the original refusal continuation, and ASR on AdvBench and JailbreakBench. Separately, on successful jailbreak prompts, restore the candidate heads by patching in their activations from the matched refusal run or scaling them up, then measure whether compliance reverts toward refusal. Compare against size-matched random head ablations and against ablations of top-activity but non-causal heads. Evaluate harmless Alpaca prompts to quantify collateral capability damage. If suppressing only the targeted subset reliably flips many refusals into compliance while random sets do not, that is strong evidence of sufficiency; if restoring those heads during jailbreak reverses compliance, that also supports necessity. If large collateral damage appears on harmless tasks, the result may indicate broad impairment rather than a specific refusal mechanism. If many more heads are required, or effects are weak and inconsistent, the "small subset is enough" subclaim is undermined. This experiment would be less necessary if there already exists a replicated dose-response demonstration showing both causal sufficiency and rescue via reactivation of the same head set.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?" separate recognition from refusal execution using a reply-inversion style design. Construct paired datasets from AdvBench harmful instructions, benign controls from Alpaca, and optionally paraphrased harmful prompts where the model is instructed to answer safely, refuse, role-play, or summarize the request rather than execute it. During successful jailbreaks and ordinary refusals, test each head or small head group for harmfulness readout power independent of the output action by decoding whether the underlying user intent is harmful from that component’s activations alone. Then ablate the previously identified refusal-mediating heads and re-measure whether harmfulness remains decodable from the remaining heads. Include a control that harmfulness decoding should not merely track toxic surface form by adding benign discussions of dangerous topics and policy-analysis prompts. If substantial harmfulness signal persists in many heads after the refusal-related subset is suppressed and even during successful jailbreak responses, that supports the claim that other heads continue representing harmful content. If harmfulness signal disappears broadly once jailbreak succeeds, then the bypass account is weakened and elimination or task reinterpretation becomes more plausible. If decoding is driven only by lexical toxicity controls, the result would not support a genuine safety-relevant representation claim. This experiment becomes less necessary if prior work has already cleanly dissociated harmful-intent recognition heads from refusal-execution heads with strong causal evidence.

To address subclaim "Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?" and "Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?" build a zero-additional-training detector from internal activations of the aligned model. Operationalize "no additional training" strictly: choose either (a) an existing direction/head statistic identified from the above causal analyses without fitting new parameters on labeled harmfulness data, or (b) nearest-centroid / template matching using a tiny fixed set of hand-chosen reference prompts rather than supervised probe training. Evaluate this detector on public harmfulness datasets such as AdvBench and JailbreakBench plus safe datasets such as Alpaca, with matched benign dangerous-topic controls. Compare token-level and prompt-level aggregation rules chosen a priori, and report AUROC, AUPRC, FPR at fixed TPR, and robustness on successful jailbreak prompts specifically. Baselines should include simple lexical toxicity filters, the model’s own refusal behavior, and a lightly trained linear probe to quantify the gap introduced by the no-training constraint. If the zero-training readout achieves strong discrimination, especially on successful jailbreaks where behavior is compliant, that supports the claim that persistent internal representations can be directly read out. If performance only emerges after fitting a supervised probe, then the no-additional-training subclaim fails even if the representations exist. If the detector works only on the same prompt templates used to discover it, distribution shift concerns remain. This experiment would be less necessary if an existing frozen-feature detector with pre-registered thresholds had already been benchmarked on standard harmfulness suites and shown to generalize across jailbreak families.

To address subclaim "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?" benchmark the zero-training internal detector from the prior experiment against public or API-accessible safety baselines such as OpenAI Moderation, LlamaGuard or comparable HuggingFace guard models, and the base model’s refusal behavior. Use a standardized evaluation suite combining AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and harmless Alpaca prompts, plus a held-out set of successful jailbreak prompts crafted on one source model and transferred to others. Measure AUROC, AUPRC, calibrated FPR/FNR, and detection accuracy specifically on prompts that elicited harmful compliance, because that is where the proposed detector is most valuable. Include judge calibration against a human-labeled subset so that evaluation labels are trustworthy, and report runtime/cost if relevant. Also test cross-model portability: derive the detector from one open model’s internal features and compare to dedicated external safety models on the same prompts. If the zero-training internal detector is competitive with dedicated safety models on overall discrimination and especially on successful jailbreak cases, the claim is supported. If it is clearly worse, brittle under transfer, or only competitive at unacceptable false-positive rates, the final subclaim is weakened. If dedicated safety models dominate except on a narrow slice, the appropriate conclusion may be that persistent representations exist but are not yet practically competitive. This experiment becomes less necessary if there is already a public benchmark directly comparing frozen internal readouts to state-of-the-art safety classifiers on the same datasets and operating points.

To address subclaim 1, what happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds, first build a paired activation-and-behavior benchmark. Use a safety-aligned open model such as Qwen2.5-Instruct, Gemma-2-It, or Llama-3-Instruct; harmful prompts from HarmBench and AdvBench; benign but safety-sensitive controls from XSTest; and jailbreak templates from JailbreakBench or StrongREJECT. For each harmful request, run the direct prompt, several jailbreak variants, and matched benign prompts while caching residual-stream states, attention head outputs, attention patterns, and logits at every layer. Label outputs as refusal or compliance using HarmBench/StrongREJECT evaluators plus a small manual audit. This establishes whether there are enough successful jailbreaks to analyze and whether the same harmful request can produce both refusal and compliance. If successful jailbreaks still show activation patterns closer to harmful direct prompts than benign prompts, that supports persistence of safety-relevant representations; if they become representation-level benign, that weakens the claim. This experiment could be unnecessary if a public activation cache already existed for the same model, prompts, jailbreaks, and verified success labels.

To address subclaims 2 and 3, whether safety-relevant internal representations are eliminated or bypassed during a successful jailbreak, train simple layer-wise and head-wise linear probes only on non-jailbroken direct prompts to distinguish harmful HarmBench/AdvBench inputs from benign XSTest or WildGuardMix inputs, then freeze the probes and evaluate them on successful jailbreak prompts from the first experiment. Also compute representation similarity between direct harmful refusals and successful jailbreaks at the instruction-final token and harmful-span tokens. If probes trained on ordinary harmful-vs-benign examples still classify successful jailbreak activations as harmful with high AUROC, while the model behavior is compliant, this supports bypass rather than elimination. If probe performance collapses to chance specifically on successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination or at least severe scrambling of the relevant representation. This experiment would be less necessary if prior work supplied frozen probes trained on clean prompts and demonstrated their performance on independently verified successful jailbreaks.

To address subclaim 4, what the jailbreak attack selectively suppresses, compare each attention head’s output norm, value-vector contribution to refusal-related logits, attention paid to harmful request spans, and causal attribution to refusal tokens across matched direct harmful refusals and successful jailbreak compliances. Use the same public prompt sets as above and identify heads whose activity or refusal-logit contribution is consistently reduced only in successful jailbreaks, not in benign prompts or failed jailbreaks. A sparse model or greedy causal-tracing search can estimate whether the affected set is small relative to all heads. If a compact, stable subset of heads is selectively downregulated across jailbreak templates and harmful categories, the suppression subclaim is supported; if suppression is diffuse, model-specific, or absent, the subclaim is weakened. This could be made unnecessary by existing head-level attribution data showing the same selective suppression pattern across public jailbreak benchmarks.

To address subclaim 5, whether suppressing a small subset of attention heads is enough to turn a refusal into compliance, perform causal interventions on the heads identified in the previous experiment. On direct harmful prompts that normally elicit refusals, ablate, scale down, or replace those heads’ outputs with their successful-jailbreak activations, and measure whether refusal rate drops and harmful compliance rises using HarmBench/StrongREJECT scoring. Conversely, on successful jailbreak prompts, restore those heads from the matched direct-refusal run or scale them back up and test whether refusals return. If suppressing only that small set reliably converts refusal to compliance and restoration reverses it, the sufficiency and bypass claims become much stronger. If behavior does not change, or requires broad multi-layer ablation, the small-subset sufficiency claim is not feasible. This experiment could be skipped only if prior causal ablation and restoration results already showed bidirectional control over refusal/compliance for the same head set.

To address subclaim 6, whether other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds, analyze non-suppressed heads separately from the suppressed subset. Train or fit head-level harmful-content probes on direct harmful versus benign prompts, then test only non-suppressed heads on successful jailbreaks; additionally use token-level activation patching or attention analysis to see whether those heads still encode or attend to the harmful request span and harmful category. If many non-suppressed heads remain predictive of harmfulness under successful jailbreaks, while the refusal-controlling heads are suppressed, this supports the claim that harmful-content representations persist elsewhere. If harmful information is lost across most heads, or survives only in the same heads whose suppression causes compliance, the claim is weakened. This experiment might be unnecessary if the probe results from experiment 2 already include sufficiently granular head-level evidence separating suppressed from non-suppressed heads.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, whether persistent representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector without additional training and at quality competitive with dedicated safety models, define a zero-training detector before looking at detector test labels. For example, use the persistent non-suppressed heads found mechanistically in earlier experiments and score inputs by a fixed statistic such as harmful-representation probe logit from the already-frozen clean-prompt probe, cosine similarity to a predeclared harmful direction, or activation magnitude in the identified harmful-content heads, with no optimization on the detector benchmark. Evaluate threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC and fixed-threshold F1 on held-out public datasets such as HarmBench validation/test, WildGuardMix, ToxicChat, XSTest, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT, including both plain and jailbroken harmful prompts. Compare against dedicated safety models such as LlamaGuard, ShieldGemma, WildGuard, and OpenAI-style moderation baselines where available. If the frozen internal readout is competitive across datasets and especially detects successful jailbreaks missed by output-based refusal cues, the detector subclaims are supported. If it requires supervised retraining, threshold tuning on labels, or performs far below dedicated models, the subclaims are weakened. This experiment would be unnecessary if a released zero-training readout and full benchmark comparison already existed for the target model and public datasets.

To address subclaim 'What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?', build a behavioral-and-activation benchmark using a public safety-aligned open model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat or Mistral-7B-Instruct, harmful/benign prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, BeaverTails, or ToxicChat on HuggingFace, and public jailbreak templates from JailbreakBench or HarmBench. For each harmful prompt, run the plain version and several jailbroken versions, label outcomes as refusal or compliance using HarmBench's classifier or Llama-Guard, and record per-layer residual streams and per-head outputs. Compare activation similarity and harmfulness evidence in successful jailbreaks versus plain harmful refusals and benign prompts, especially at tokens where the model has enough context to recognize the request. If harmful-request signatures remain similar in successful jailbreaks while downstream refusal-generation signatures change, this supports 'bypass' rather than 'elimination'; if harmful signatures disappear or become benign-like, it supports elimination. This experiment could be made unnecessary by public activation traces showing matched plain-harmful, jailbroken-harmful, and benign examples with outcome labels across the same models.

To address subclaim 'What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?', perform head-wise causal tracing and activation-difference analysis on the successful-jailbreak subset from Experiment 1. For every attention head, measure changes in output norm, residual contribution, attention pattern, and causal effect on attack success rate when patching head activations between plain harmful refusal runs and successful jailbreak runs. Prioritize heads whose jailbroken activations are consistently reduced and whose restoration from the plain harmful run decreases compliance. If only a small number of middle-to-late heads show both suppression and large causal restoration effects, this supports the claim that the attack selectively suppresses a small subset of safety-relevant heads; if suppression is diffuse or restoration has little effect, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a replicated head-level path-patching table from the cited continuation-triggered jailbreak paper covering the same attacks, models, and datasets.

To address subclaim 'Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?', take the candidate suppressed safety heads from Experiment 2 and intervene during generation on plain harmful prompts that the model normally refuses. Zero or scale down only those heads at relevant positions, then measure refusal rate, attack success rate, and answer harmfulness with HarmBench or Llama-Guard; compare against equal-size random head sets, high-activation non-safety heads, and ablations of continuation heads. If suppressing the identified subset alone reliably converts refusals into compliant responses at a much higher rate than controls, the subclaim is supported; if it only weakly changes behavior or requires broad ablation, the subclaim is not supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by an existing causal ablation study showing that the same head subset is sufficient, not merely correlated, to flip refusal into compliance.

To address subclaim 'Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?', first identify heads or residual directions that encode harmfulness on non-jailbroken harmful-versus-benign prompts using training-free diagnostics such as logit-lens projection to fixed labels like unsafe/safe, cosine similarity to fixed label-token embeddings, or causal patching from harmful into benign contexts. Then test those same heads or directions on successful jailbreak runs without refitting anything. Also patch the non-suppressed heads from successful jailbreak runs into benign prompts to see whether they increase harmfulness/readout scores while leaving the suppressed safety-head intervention separate. If non-suppressed heads continue to score jailbroken harmful prompts as harmful and their activations are closer to plain harmful than benign prompts, this supports persistent harmful-content representation; if all heads become benign-like during jailbreak success, it argues against persistence. This experiment could be made unnecessary by head-level representational analyses showing that harmfulness information remains decodable from non-ablated heads during successful jailbreaks.

To address subclaim 'Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?' and 'Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?', construct a strictly zero-training detector from the persistent heads found above. For example, score an input by aggregating the selected heads' direct logit-lens or unembedding contributions to a fixed, predeclared set of unsafe/refusal label tokens versus safe/benign label tokens, with no learned probe, no gradient updates, and no fitted weights; evaluate ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, false-positive rate at fixed recall, and calibration on held-out public datasets such as HarmBench, ToxicChat, BeaverTails, and JailbreakBench. If this frozen readout separates harmful from benign and jailbroken harmful inputs substantially above chance, the direct-readout/no-additional-training subclaims are supported; if it requires a learned linear probe or extensive calibration to work, the 'no additional training' part is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a released implementation and evaluation logs for a zero-shot internal-activation harmfulness detector on these public benchmarks.

To address subclaim 'How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?', benchmark the zero-training internal readout from Experiment 5 against public dedicated safety models and classifiers such as Llama-Guard-2/3, ShieldGemma, HarmBench's classifier, and Detoxify on the same frozen splits from HarmBench, JailbreakBench, ToxicChat, and BeaverTails. Use identical input text, identical outcome definitions, and report ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, recall at low false-positive rates, robustness on successful jailbreak prompts, latency, and compute overhead. If the internal readout is within a small margin of dedicated models overall and especially strong on jailbreak-obfuscated harmful prompts, the 'competitive quality' part of the claim is supported; if it trails substantially or fails on benign edge cases, the claim should be narrowed. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a peer-reviewed head-to-head benchmark using the same public datasets, open model, and no-training readout constraints.

To address subclaim 'What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?', first establish a reproducible behavioral and activation dataset. Run public harmful-instruction sets such as AdvBench and JailbreakBench, plus benign controls from Alpaca, on open safety-aligned models such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-2-13B-Chat, and another chat-tuned open model if resources allow. For each harmful instruction, evaluate both the plain prompt and standardized jailbreak variants such as JailbreakBench templates or GCG-generated suffixes, using deterministic decoding and fixed max_new_tokens. Label refusal versus compliance with a judge chosen on a held-out human-labeled subset, and manually audit a sample. Save residual-stream, MLP, and attention-head activations for matched triples: benign prompt, harmful prompt that is refused, and the same harmful intent under a successful jailbreak. If successful jailbreaks are rare or judging is unreliable, the central claim cannot be tested cleanly on that model/attack pair; if there are many matched refused-versus-jailbroken examples, later causal and readout experiments become meaningful. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a public release containing matched prompts, success labels, human-audited judgments, and full activation traces for the same model family.

To address subclaims 'Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?' and 'Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?', test whether harmfulness information remains linearly and geometrically available in activations during successful attacks. Train only diagnostic probes on clean refused harmful prompts versus benign Alpaca prompts using a training split of AdvBench/JailbreakBench, then evaluate those probes, without updating them, on held-out successful jailbreak prompts with the same harmful intent. Also compute representation similarity and nearest-neighbor structure between clean harmful/refused activations, jailbroken/successful activations, and benign activations layer by layer. Strong evidence against elimination would be that probes trained on clean harmful/refused states still classify successful jailbreak states as harmful, and that those states remain closer to clean harmful states than to benign states in many layers or components. Evidence for elimination would be probe collapse to chance and representation movement toward benign states specifically on successful jailbreaks. Evidence for bypass would be persistence of harmfulness information together with behavioral compliance and weakened refusal-generation signals. This experiment could be made unnecessary by published layerwise probe and similarity results showing the same clean-harmful-to-jailbreak information preservation under deterministic decoding.

To address subclaim 'What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?', identify whether successful jailbreaks consistently reduce the contribution of a small subset of attention heads. Using the matched activation dataset, compare each attention head’s output norm, attention pattern, residual-stream contribution, and direct effect on refusal-related logits between clean harmful/refused prompts and successful jailbreak prompts. Then run attribution patching or ACDC-style threshold sweeps from output to input to find heads whose clean-to-jailbreak activation changes best explain the refusal-to-compliance behavioral shift, and compare against simple baselines such as ranking by activation norm alone. Include size-matched random head sets and benign-prompt controls. The claim is supported if a sparse, stable set of heads shows selective suppression during jailbreaks, has high patching attribution for refusal loss, and is much more predictive than random sets; it is weakened if changes are diffuse across many heads, equally present on benign prompts, or indistinguishable from random sparsification. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a public circuit-discovery artifact reporting head-level suppression statistics, threshold sweeps, and random-ablation controls on the same benchmarks.

To address subclaim 'Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?', perform causal interventions on the candidate suppressed heads found in the previous experiment. On plain harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, zero or scale down only the candidate heads at inference and measure ASR, refusal rate, KL divergence from baseline, and harmless-task performance on Alpaca. In the reverse direction, on successful jailbreak prompts, patch or scale the candidate heads back toward their clean harmful/refused activations and measure whether refusals return. Use deterministic decoding, size-matched random head ablations, all-attention-head ablation as a positive degradation control, and unmodified inference as the baseline. The subclaim is supported if suppressing the candidate heads alone substantially converts refusals into relevant harmful compliance while random head sets do not, and if restoring those heads in jailbroken runs reduces ASR; it is weakened if the intervention only causes incoherence, broad capability loss, or effects no larger than random ablations. This experiment could be made unnecessary by published bidirectional causal-ablation and activation-patching results demonstrating both sufficiency and reversibility for the same small head set.

To address subclaim 'Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?', analyze non-suppressed heads separately from the candidate bypass heads. For each attention head, train or evaluate diagnostic harmful-versus-benign readouts on clean refused harmful prompts and benign Alpaca prompts, then test on successful jailbreak prompts; additionally test whether zeroing the suppressed subset leaves harmfulness readout accuracy in the remaining heads largely intact. Use per-head AUROC, mutual-information estimates, and representation similarity to map where harmful content remains available. The subclaim is supported if many non-suppressed heads continue to carry harmfulness information on successful jailbreaks even while the suppressed subset controls refusal behavior; it is weakened if harmfulness information is localized only in the suppressed heads or disappears broadly during successful jailbreaks. This also helps discriminate harmfulness recognition from refusal execution: persistent harmful readouts in non-suppressed heads plus causal refusal control in suppressed heads would support bypass rather than erasure. This experiment could be made unnecessary by an existing head-level atlas showing persistent harmful-content decodability outside the refusal-control heads during successful attacks.

To address subclaims 'Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?', 'Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?', and 'How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?', build a detector from the persistent representations identified above and evaluate it on held-out AdvBench/JailbreakBench harmful prompts, jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompts, and Alpaca benign prompts. Include a strict no-training variant, such as a pre-specified scalar score from frozen model activations or direct-logit-lens contributions of persistent heads to safety/refusal-related token sets, reporting threshold-free AUROC and AUPRC; optionally include a threshold calibrated on a small validation split but no learned weights. Compare against dedicated safety baselines such as LlamaGuard, OpenAI Moderation if available, and other public moderation classifiers, using the same human-audited labels and reporting FPR at fixed TPR as well as aggregate AUROC. The strong version of the claim is supported if the no-training activation readout is statistically competitive with dedicated safety models, especially on jailbreak-wrapped harmful inputs; a weaker version is supported if a lightly calibrated or trained probe is competitive; the no-additional-training subclaim is falsified if only a trained classifier works. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a public benchmark comparing frozen internal-activation readouts with dedicated safety models on the same harmful, jailbroken, and benign datasets with human-validated labels.

To address subclaims 1–3 concerning whether safety-relevant representations are eliminated or bypassed, run paired forward passes on open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it using harmful prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench. For each harmful request, retain the plain version and one or more jailbreak variants that are verified to change refusal into substantive compliance by the HarmBench evaluator plus a blinded human audit; include benign prompts matched for topic, vocabulary, and jailbreak-template style. Record residual-stream states and individual attention-head outputs at every layer and token. Train diagnostic probes only on plain harmful versus benign prompts, freeze them, and test cross-condition decoding on successful jailbreaks; also measure representational similarity and harmfulness-direction projections between plain and jailbroken versions. Above-chance, well-calibrated cross-decoding across models and unseen attack families would show that harmfulness information persists, favoring bypass over elimination; collapse to benign-level decoding throughout the network would support elimination, while persistence only in early layers would weaken the broad claim. Public release of equivalent paired activations and preregistered cross-attack analyses could make rerunning this experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaim 4, that a jailbreak selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, use the successful paired cases from Experiment 1 to quantify, for every head, changes in output norm, attention pattern, and projection onto the clean harmfulness/refusal direction at matched semantic token positions. Fit a hierarchical model across prompts, attacks, layers, and model families, with false-discovery control, and compare the concentration of suppression with random-head, benign-template, prompt-length, and token-position controls. Define 'small' prospectively, for example as at most 1% of all heads explaining at least 50% of the attack-associated reduction in the refusal-direction signal, and test whether the same heads recur across held-out prompts and attack families. Concentrated, reproducible suppression specific to successful attacks would support the subclaim; diffuse changes, inconsistent head identities, or equally strong suppression on benign template controls would refute or substantially qualify it. Published head-level causal or activation data covering the same models and controls could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaim 5, that suppressing the identified small subset of heads is by itself sufficient to turn refusal into compliance, causally intervene on plain harmful prompts from held-out HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench splits. Zero, scale down, or replace only the candidate heads' safety-direction components with their values from matched successful-jailbreak runs while leaving all other activations unchanged; score substantive compliance using the HarmBench evaluator and blinded human review. Compare against equal-size random head sets, heads matched by activation norm or layer, full-head versus direction-only ablation, and interventions on benign tasks from MMLU and AlpacaEval to detect generic model damage. Test necessity as a complementary intervention by restoring the clean-prompt safety component in those heads during successful jailbreaks. A large and reproducible refusal-to-compliance shift from candidate-head suppression, together with restored refusal under reverse patching and little benign degradation, would establish sufficiency and support bypass; no shift, effects requiring many heads, or nonspecific incoherence would reject the strong causal claim. Existing public intervention results with code, exact head sets, and random-head controls could make this test unnecessary.

To address subclaim 6, that other attention heads continue representing harmful content during successful jailbreaks, remove the causally implicated subset from all analyses and test each remaining head and prespecified layer-wise aggregates for harmfulness information. Train linear probes on plain HarmBench or AdvBench harmful prompts versus topic- and style-matched benign examples, freeze all weights and thresholds, and evaluate only on successful jailbreaks from unseen JailbreakBench attack families; use label permutation, minimum-description-length probing, low-rank controls, and lexical adversarial examples to ensure that decoding is not due merely to keywords or probe capacity. Also patch the harmfulness-direction component from these remaining heads into benign matched prompts to distinguish decodable information from causal control of refusal. Robust decoding from many nonimplicated heads, despite their inability to restore refusal individually, would show that harmful content remains represented while the behavior-control pathway is bypassed; disappearance of decodability after removing the suppressed subset would contradict the claim. A sufficiently broad public head-wise decoding study on successful, behavior-verified jailbreaks could replace this experiment.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, concerning direct harmful-input detection without additional training, preregister a genuinely zero-training readout before examining detector labels. For example, at a fixed layer chosen independently of safety data, score the residual stream or noncausal-head aggregate by its cosine projection onto the model's own unembedding-vector contrast for fixed words such as 'harmful' minus 'harmless', use zero as the fixed threshold, and fit no probe, head weights, or threshold. Separately report a weaker 'no gradient training' variant that uses the head subset discovered in Experiments 2–4 and a benign-only quantile threshold, clearly labeling this as calibrated rather than strictly training-free. Evaluate both on held-out HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and benign WildChat or LMSYS-Chat-1M examples, including unseen jailbreak families, multilingual items where available, and topic-matched benign controls. Strong AUROC and useful fixed-threshold sensitivity and specificity for the strict rule would support direct zero-training readout; success only after supervised head selection, label-based thresholding, or probe fitting would refute the 'no additional training' wording while possibly supporting a weaker low-training claim. A fully specified, frozen readout released before evaluation on these datasets could make this experiment largely unnecessary.

To address subclaim 9, that the representation-based detector is competitive with dedicated safety models, benchmark the frozen detector from Experiment 5 against public dedicated safeguards such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and the HarmBench classifier on identical, contamination-audited test sets from HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, WildChat or LMSYS-Chat-1M, and multilingual safety datasets available on Hugging Face. Report AUROC, AUPRC under realistic class imbalance, recall at 1% and 5% false-positive rates, expected calibration error, per-category and per-attack-family performance, bootstrap confidence intervals, latency, memory, and whether access to the generator's internal activations gives an operational cost advantage. Freeze every method before testing and include cross-model transfer, testing whether a readout identified in one generator works in another, as a stringent robustness check. Statistically noninferior safety performance across unseen attacks and categories, with comparable false-positive rates and lower incremental cost, would justify 'competitive'; superiority only on the same model or attacks used to identify heads would indicate overfitting, and materially worse low-FPR recall would reject the claim. Public, independently reproduced head-to-head evaluations using the same frozen splits and metrics could obviate this final benchmark.

To address subclaims 1–4, build a paired activation dataset for successful jailbreaks. Run open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on harmful requests from the public HarmBench and JailbreakBench datasets, both without an attack and with public attack templates from JailbreakBench; add benign and borderline examples from PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails and WildGuardMix. Retain matched cases in which the original request is refused but the attacked version is judged compliant by both a public HarmBench evaluator and blinded human review. Record every head output, attention pattern, residual-stream state, and next-token refusal/compliance logits at matched semantic positions. Test whether successful attacks produce concentrated reductions in the activation norms or safety-token logit contributions of a small number of heads, while harmfulness information remains decodable elsewhere using a preregistered zero-shot harmful-versus-benign verbalizer score. Concentrated suppression with persistent harmfulness signals would support bypass; disappearance of harmfulness signals throughout the network would support elimination; diffuse changes would reject the selective-head account. This observational screen identifies candidates but cannot establish causality, so it informs the following interventions.

To address subclaims 3 and 4, causally test whether successful jailbreaks bypass refusal by suppressing a small head set. On the matched cases from Experiment 1, use head-level path patching between the refused and successfully attacked runs: patch each attacked head output with its refusal-run counterpart and perform the reverse patch, initially one head at a time and then with sparse combinations. Validate that the relevant difference is suppression by continuously scaling each candidate head from its attacked activation toward its refusal activation, rather than relying only on zero ablation. Preregister ‘small subset’ as at most 1% of all heads accounting for at least 80% of the recoverable change in attack-success rate or refusal-logit margin, and compare against random, activation-norm-matched, and layer-matched head sets. If restoring a sparse set reliably reinstates refusal and reverse patching promotes compliance, the results support selective suppression and bypass; weak or distributed mediation would contradict that mechanism. Full per-example patching results and activations from the cited continuation-triggered-jailbreak paper could reduce the need to reproduce its narrow result, but not the need to test broader attacks and models.

To address subclaim 5, test whether suppressing the identified safety heads is by itself sufficient to convert an ordinary refusal into compliance. Apply zeroing and graded down-scaling of the locked head set to un-attacked harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, while leaving prompts and all other activations unchanged. Measure transition rates from refusal to substantive compliance, generated-content harmfulness, perplexity, and benign-task utility; include equally sized random-head sets, high-norm heads, continuation heads, and all-head perturbations with matched total intervention norm. Also test held-out harmful categories from HarmBench so sufficiency is not defined on the discovery examples. A large, dose-dependent refusal-to-compliance transition caused only by the sparse safety-head intervention, with little benign degradation, would support sufficiency; merely shortening refusals, producing incoherence, or requiring many heads would refute or narrow the claim. Published intervention code, exact head lists, and held-out ablation results could make a direct replication less necessary, although independent controls would still be valuable.

To address subclaims 2 and 6, determine whether non-suppressed heads continue to represent harmful content during successful attacks. Exclude the causally identified safety heads and evaluate the remaining individual heads and residual pathways using two assays: a zero-shot logit-lens harmful-versus-benign verbalizer score requiring no fitted parameters, and cross-validated diagnostic probes used only as scientific measurement. Train any diagnostic probes on unattacked HarmBench and BeaverTails examples, then test without adaptation on successful JailbreakBench attacks; include shuffled-label, token-overlap-matched, benign-jailbreak-template, and cross-category controls. Compare decoding accuracy and representational similarity before and after attack at matched positions, and test whether the signal survives removal of the strongest few non-safety heads. Above-chance, cross-attack decoding from many untouched heads would show that harmfulness representations persist despite compliance and favor bypass over elimination; chance-level results under well-powered controls would favor elimination or indicate that the information moved to an unmeasured representation. Public release of complete attacked-run activations with equivalent controls could substitute for collecting new activations.

To address subclaims 7–9, benchmark a genuinely training-free harmful-input detector built from the persistent representations. Before examining test labels, lock the model layers or heads, harmful and safe verbalizer token sets, aggregation rule, and a zero-centered decision rule based on Experiments 1–4; do not fit a probe, threshold, calibration layer, or model weights on the target datasets. Evaluate both the strict version, whose head list and rule transfer from a separate discovery model, and the weaker version in which mechanistic head selection is allowed but no detector parameters are learned. Test on held-out splits of HarmBench, JailbreakBench, WildGuardMix, and PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails, reporting AUROC, AUPRC, balanced accuracy at the fixed threshold, calibration, category-wise recall, and false positives on benign prompts containing superficially dangerous vocabulary. Compare under identical input access with public dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard 3, WildGuard, and ShieldGemma. Competitive performance, with confidence intervals overlapping the dedicated models and robustness to successful jailbreak wrappers, would substantiate direct training-free readout; performance requiring labeled threshold tuning or materially below the baselines would refute the strongest claim. Existing public evaluations would make this experiment unnecessary only if they expose the exact no-training protocol, frozen rule, test examples, and comparable baseline outputs.

To address the claimed generality of all subclaims, perform a preregistered transfer study across at least three open model families, multiple sizes where feasible, and distinct attack families from HarmBench and JailbreakBench, including continuation-triggered, role-play, encoding or obfuscation, and optimization-based attacks. Freeze the head-selection criterion, sparsity definition, intervention strength, and detector construction before moving from the first model to the others; account for differing head counts by using layer-relative locations and normalized effect sizes rather than manually choosing new favorable heads. For each model and attack family, jointly report selective-suppression concentration, causal refusal recovery, sufficiency of sparse suppression, persistence of harmfulness information in other heads, and zero-training detector performance. Consistent effects would support a model-family-level mechanism; effects confined to continuation attacks or one architecture would show that the evidence supports only a narrow claim rather than jailbreaks generally. A sufficiently broad public multi-model replication with released activations, interventions, and preregistered analyses could replace this transfer study.

To address subclaims 1–3, create paired runs on open safety-aligned models such as Llama-2-Chat, Llama-3-Instruct, and Mistral-Instruct using public harmful instructions from AdvBench and JailbreakBench, harmless instructions from Alpaca, and several established jailbreak methods, including GCG and public JailbreakBench templates. Retain only pairs where the ordinary harmful prompt is refused but the jailbroken version receives a relevant harmful response, as determined under greedy decoding by an automated judge calibrated against 100–200 human-labeled outputs. At every layer and attention head, measure whether harmfulness remains decodable from the input-token activations using cross-validated linear probes trained on disjoint ordinary harmful versus harmless prompts, then test those probes without refitting on successful jailbreaks. Include benign prompts wrapped in the same jailbreak templates and paraphrase-matched harmful prompts as controls. Persistently high held-out AUROC on successful jailbreaks, despite a reversal from refusal to compliance, would reject elimination and support persistence; a broad collapse to chance would support elimination. Persistence alone would not prove bypass, so this experiment should determine the representations and examples used by the subsequent causal tests. It could be shortened if public checkpoints, paired prompts, outputs, and full activation traces demonstrating the same result across models were available.

To address subclaim 4, identify what the attack selectively suppresses by comparing each attention head’s activation norm, refusal-logit contribution, harmfulness-probe score, and path-patching effect between ordinary harmful prompts and their successful jailbroken counterparts. Apply ACDC with a threshold sweep and matched SP/HISP rankings, and require candidate heads to show consistent suppression across held-out instructions and at least two attack families rather than merely low activation. Compare against harmless prompts with identical jailbreak wrappers, failed jailbreaks, and semantically changed prompts; use interchange patching as well as zero replacement to control for corruption choice. A sparse, reproducible group of heads whose refusal-related contribution falls specifically during successful attacks would support selective suppression, whereas diffuse changes, attack-specific sets, or equal suppression on benign wrapped prompts would weaken the claim. Released head-level activation and causal-patching data with these controls could make new discovery runs unnecessary.

To address subclaim 5 and the causal portion of subclaim 3, test whether the candidate head subset is sufficient to switch behavior. On ordinary harmful prompts that are normally refused, zero or continuously scale the selected heads from 1 to 0 and measure refusal-to-compliance transitions, ASR, response relevance, and output KL under greedy decoding. Perform the converse intervention on successful jailbreaks by restoring clean-run head activations through activation patching or scaling the heads above baseline, testing whether refusal returns. Controls must include baseline inference, size-matched random heads over many draws, heads chosen only by activation magnitude, sham patching from the same condition, and Alpaca prompts to measure general capability damage. A large, dose-dependent compliance increase from suppressing only the selected heads, together with restored refusal under reverse patching and little benign degradation, would provide strong evidence of sufficiency and bypass; effects matched by random ablations or accompanied by broad incoherence would favor generic model damage. Existing preregistered intervention results across multiple checkpoints could obviate repetition on those checkpoints.

To address subclaim 6, localize the representations that survive outside the suppressed subset. Train head-local harmfulness probes only on ordinary harmful versus harmless inputs, freeze them, and evaluate each head on held-out successful jailbreaks; additionally use path patching into two separate tasks: harmful-input recognition with a forced-choice harmful/harmless answer and refusal execution or reply inversion with harmfulness held constant. Then ablate the suppressed subset and ask whether non-suppressed heads retain high harmfulness AUROC even when the generated answer becomes compliant. Include label-permuted probes, layer- and width-matched random heads, failed jailbreaks, benign jailbreak-wrapped prompts, and multiple activation positions. If many non-suppressed heads continue to encode harmfulness while only the small suppressed set controls refusal, the results would distinguish recognition from refusal execution and support bypass; if harmfulness information vanishes globally or only refusal-correlated heads decode it, the claim would be weakened. Public head-wise probe scores and recognition-versus-execution patching results on the same datasets could replace this experiment.

To address subclaims 7–9, construct a strictly training-free detector from the persistent representations found above: freeze the model and selected heads, project their residual-stream contributions onto a prespecified harmful-versus-harmless verbalizer direction derived from the model’s own output embeddings, combine heads with an equal-weight rule, and fit no probe weights. Report threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC and, separately, F1, false-positive rate, and false-negative rate using a threshold fixed on a public development split. Evaluate on disjoint AdvBench and JailbreakBench attacks, Alpaca harmless prompts, unseen jailbreak families, and benign prompts containing sensitive vocabulary. Compare under identical examples with public dedicated safeguards such as LlamaGuard and ShieldGemma, plus OpenAI Moderation if API access is permitted; report latency and memory as secondary metrics. Competitive held-out discrimination without learned parameters would support direct readout and the no-additional-training claim, while performance requiring fitted weights, collapsing on unseen attacks, or trailing safety models substantially would refute one or more subclaims. A released immutable scoring rule and independently reproduced benchmark predictions could make rerunning this comparison unnecessary.

To address the claimed generality of all subclaims, preregister a replication across several independently aligned open model families and sizes, using attacks generated on one source model and transferred to the others. Repeat the paired-representation test, sparse-head discovery, bidirectional causal intervention, and frozen detector evaluation with identical greedy decoding and a judge selected before analysis through comparison with human-majority labels. Report per-model and per-attack effects with bootstrap confidence intervals, head-set overlap after architecture-aware alignment, random-ablation distributions, and defended results using public guardrails where feasible. Consistent representation persistence, sparse causal suppression, and competitive direct detection across families would support a general mechanism; replication in only one checkpoint would instead indicate a model-specific circuit, and high behavioral transfer without mechanistic transfer would show that different models can be jailbroken through different internal routes. This replication could be reduced if independent groups release equivalent multi-family results, code, prompts, labels, and activation traces.
